intro: In a busy New York churchyard, an old gravestone carries a line of tiny shapes. In a green and gold book from the 1700s, page after page is filled with symbols nobody could read. Both hold real messages. Both were made by members of secret societies who wanted to share words with each other, and keep them from everyone else.

In this unit, you will become a codebreaker. You will learn the pigpen cipher and read the message on James Leeson's stone. You will count letters the way codebreakers have for more than a thousand years. You will follow three researchers who used computers and language skills to crack the Copiale Cipher in 2011.

You will also meet stonemasons in Scotland who were tested on their memory in 1599. By the end, you will be able to make and break a simple cipher, explain how a key works, and build a memory palace of your own. You will also practice asking: what does the evidence really show?
bigQuestion: Why did secret societies hide their words in codes, and how do people unlock them?

timeline.t: Julius Caesar sends private letters in a shift cipher, a Roman writer later reports.
In Baghdad, al-Kindi writes the oldest known guide to breaking ciphers by counting letters.
Agrippa's book shows letters hidden in a grid, an early ancestor of pigpen.
William Schaw writes his first rules for Scottish stonemasons' lodges.
Schaw's second rules tell the Kilwinning lodge to test masons on the art of memory.
Freemasons use the pigpen cipher widely, and it becomes known as the Masonic cipher.
Someone writes the Copiale Cipher, a 105-page book of symbols and letters.
James Leeson dies; his New York gravestone carries a pigpen line.
A Masonic ceremony book is written in cipher as a private study aid.
Kevin Knight, Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer crack the Copiale Cipher.

title: Codebreakers

chapters.title: Codes on Stones and in Books
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a message be hidden in plain sight, and how do people figure out what it says?

story.title: Shapes on an Old Stone
story.kicker: A visitor in a busy New York churchyard spots a row of strange shapes carved on a gravestone.
paragraphs: It is a bright fall day in New York City. Tall office towers rise on every side. Cars and buses rush along Broadway. A girl we will call Rosa walks through a gate with her aunt. Suddenly the street noise feels far away. They are in Trinity Churchyard, one of the oldest burial grounds in the city.

Old gray gravestones lean in the grass. Most of them show names and dates. Rosa stops at one small stone. It belongs to a man named James Leeson. He died in 1794. Near the top is a carving of a square and a compass. Rosa's aunt says that is a sign of the Freemasons, a very old club of friends.

Then Rosa sees something odd. Along one edge is a row of little shapes. Some look like boxes with open sides. Some look like the letter V turned in different ways. A few have tiny dots inside. "Is that a secret language?" Rosa asks. Her aunt smiles. "It is a code. And we can learn to read it."

Rosa's aunt draws two tic-tac-toe grids and two big X shapes in a notebook. She writes letters of the alphabet inside the spaces. Rosa matches the first shape on the stone to a space in the grid. It is the letter R. Then E. Then M. Letter by letter, a message appears.

Rosa is a made-up visitor. But the stone is real. You can still see it in the churchyard today. In this chapter, you will learn the code that is carved on it. You will also learn how people break codes they have never seen before.
story.think: Why do you think someone would carve a message in code on a gravestone, where anyone can see it?

lessons.title: Letters in Little Pens
lessons.mainIdea: The pigpen cipher swaps each letter for the shape of the space it sits in on a grid or an X.
reading: Picture a farm. Pigs live in small fenced areas called pens. The *pigpen cipher* gets its name from that idea. Each letter of the alphabet lives in its own little pen. To write a letter in code, you draw the shape of its pen instead of the letter.

Here is one common way to set it up. Draw a tic-tac-toe grid and put A through I in its nine spaces. Draw a second grid with a dot in each space for J through R. Then draw a big X for S, T, U and V. A second X with dots holds W, X, Y and Z.

Now look at the letter A. It sits in the top left corner of the first grid. Its pen has a line on the right and a line on the bottom. So A is written as a shape like a backward L. Every letter gets a shape this way. There are other versions of the key, so the letters may sit in a different order.

words.d: a secret alphabet where each letter is written as the shape of its space on a grid or an X
a way of hiding a message by changing each letter into another letter or symbol

look.title: Draw the Key
look.text: Draw a tic-tac-toe grid. Write A, B, C in the top row, D, E, F in the middle row and G, H, I in the bottom row. Look at the middle space, where E lives. It has lines on all four sides. So in pigpen, E is written as a small closed box.
look.prompt: Using the same grid, what shape would you draw for the letter C? Describe which sides have lines.

check.q: Where does the pigpen cipher get its name?
choices: From a famous code maker named Pig
From pens on a farm, because each letter sits in its own little pen
From the pens people use for writing
check.why: The reading says the name comes from farm pens. Each letter lives in its own pen, or space.

check.q: In pigpen, what do you draw instead of a letter?
choices: The shape of the letter's space on the grid or X
check.why: In the pigpen cipher, each letter is written as the shape of the space it sits in.

check.q: In the common key, how is the second grid different from the first grid?
choices: It has a dot in each space
It has no lines at all
It is shaped like a star
check.why: The reading says the second grid has a dot in each space. The dots show that the letter comes from J through R.

lessons.title: An Old Idea, a Masonic Name
lessons.mainIdea: Pigpen is older than the Freemasons, but Freemasons used it so much that it is often called the Masonic cipher.
reading: Many people say the Freemasons invented pigpen. The *Freemasons* are a brotherhood that began with stonemasons, the workers who built with stone. Their lodges, or clubs, grew in Britain in the 1600s and 1700s. But the idea of hiding letters in a grid is older than their lodges.

In the 1530s, a German writer named Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa published a big book about hidden knowledge. Scholars agree it shows letters placed in a grid of boxes. Historians see this grid as an early ancestor of pigpen. That book came out long before the first grand lodge of Freemasons.

So the Freemasons did not invent the grid. They took it up and spread it. Masons used it widely from the 1700s. That is why pigpen is also called the Masonic cipher or the Freemasons' cipher. A name can tell you who used a thing most, not who made it first.

words.d: a brotherhood that grew out of groups of stonemasons; its members meet in lodges
an older thing or person that a newer one comes from

look.title: Two Claims Side by Side
look.text: Claim 1: "The Freemasons invented the pigpen cipher." Claim 2: "A grid for hiding letters appears in Agrippa's book from the 1530s. Freemasons used a version of it widely from the 1700s."
look.prompt: Which claim fits the evidence of dates better? Explain how the dates help you decide.

check.q: Why is pigpen sometimes called the Masonic cipher?
choices: Because a Mason carved the first one in 1530
Because it is only allowed inside lodges
Because Freemasons used it widely from the 1700s
Because it uses the square and compass
check.why: The reading says Masons took up the cipher and used it widely, so it got their name.

check.q: What does Agrippa's book from the 1530s show?
choices: Letters placed in a grid of boxes
check.why: Scholars agree Agrippa's book shows letters in a grid, an early ancestor of pigpen.

check.q: What lesson about names does this story teach?
choices: A name always tells who made a thing
Names of codes are always secret
A name can tell who used a thing most, not who made it first
check.why: The Masonic cipher is named for the Masons who used it, even though the grid idea is older.

lessons.title: Codes and Ciphers
lessons.mainIdea: A code swaps whole words, a cipher swaps letters, and both turn plain words into hidden ones.
reading: People often say "code" for any secret message. Codebreakers use two words. A *code* swaps a whole word or idea for something else. For example, a team might agree that "pizza" means "meet at the gym." You need the list of meanings to understand it.

A cipher works on single letters. Each letter is changed into another letter or a symbol. Pigpen is a cipher, because every letter gets its own shape. You can hide any word with a cipher, even a word nobody planned for.

The message you start with is called *plaintext*. It is the plain words anyone can read. After you hide it, it is called ciphertext. Changing plaintext into ciphertext is called enciphering. Changing it back is called deciphering. Many people also say encode and decode.

words.d: a system that swaps whole words or ideas for other words or signs
the message in plain words before it is hidden
the message after it has been hidden with a cipher

look.title: Code or Cipher?
look.text: Message A: A coach tells the team that "blue" means "run to the left." Message B: A student writes her name with every letter turned into a pigpen shape.
look.prompt: Which message uses a code, and which uses a cipher? What clue helped you tell them apart?

check.q: What is the difference between a code and a cipher?
choices: A code uses numbers and a cipher uses colors
A code swaps whole words, and a cipher swaps single letters
A code is new and a cipher is very old
There is no difference at all
check.why: The reading says a code swaps whole words or ideas, and a cipher changes each letter.

check.q: What is plaintext?
choices: A message written on plain paper
A message that has been hidden
The message in plain words before it is hidden
check.why: Plaintext is the plain message anyone can read, before it is hidden.

check.q: Why is pigpen called a cipher and not a code?
choices: Because every single letter gets its own shape
Because it only works for one word
Because it was made by a coach
Because it uses a list of meanings
check.why: Pigpen changes each letter into a shape, which is what a cipher does.

lessons.title: A Stone in Trinity Churchyard
lessons.mainIdea: James Leeson, who died in 1794, has a gravestone in New York with a line carved in the pigpen cipher.
reading: Trinity Church stands on Broadway at Wall Street in Lower Manhattan. Around it is an old churchyard, a burial ground next to a church. People have been buried there since the 1600s. Today it sits among tall office buildings.

One stone belongs to James Leeson, who died in 1794. The stone shows a square and a compass. That is a well-known *symbol* of the Freemasons. It tells us Leeson was likely a Mason, or his friends wanted to honor the Masons. The stone also has other carvings often seen on old graves.

Across the stone runs a line of small shapes. They are letters in the pigpen cipher. Anyone who knows the key can read them. Many visitors walk right past without noticing. That is part of what makes it a good *mystery* for a codebreaker.

words.d: a picture or shape that stands for an idea or a group
something that is hard to understand or not yet explained

look.title: The Leeson Gravestone
look.text: A small upright gravestone for James Leeson, who died in 1794. It is carved with the Masonic square and compass and other grave carvings. A line of pigpen shapes runs across it. When decoded, the shapes read REMEMBER DEATH.
look.cite: James Leeson gravestone, Trinity Churchyard, New York, 1794 (described from photographs; see Atlas Obscura, "Trinity Churchyard")
look.prompt: Which parts of this stone could anyone understand, and which part needs a key? Explain.

check.q: Where is James Leeson's gravestone?
choices: In Trinity Churchyard in New York City
check.why: The reading says the stone is in the churchyard of Trinity Church, on Broadway at Wall Street.

check.q: What does the square and compass on the stone stand for?
check.why: The reading says the square and compass is a well-known symbol of the Freemasons.

check.q: Who can read the line of shapes on the stone?
choices: Anyone who knows the pigpen key
No one, because it has never been solved
check.why: The shapes are pigpen letters, so anyone who knows the key can read them.

lessons.title: Remember Death
lessons.mainIdea: The pigpen line on the Leeson stone reads REMEMBER DEATH, an old reminder that life is short and precious.
reading: When you decode the shapes on the Leeson stone, they spell REMEMBER DEATH. You can check this yourself. Match each shape to its pen in the key. The letters line up one by one. Many writers and codebreakers have checked it the same way.

The words may sound gloomy at first. But they were a very common message in those days. People called this kind of reminder by a Latin name, *memento mori*. It means "remember that you will die." The idea was to live well, be kind and use your time wisely.

Old gravestones in Europe and America often carried this message. Some showed an hourglass, with sand running out. Leeson's stone says the same thing in a quieter way. Only people who knew the cipher could read it at a glance.

words.d: Latin words meaning "remember that you will die"; a reminder to live well
to turn a hidden message back into plain words

look.title: Letters in the Stone's Message
look.cite: Letter count of the decoded line REMEMBER DEATH, James Leeson gravestone, Trinity Churchyard, New York (1794)
look.prompt: Which letter shows up most in this short message? Why might that help a codebreaker who did not have the key?

check.q: What does the pigpen line on the Leeson stone say?
check.why: When the shapes are decoded with the key, they spell REMEMBER DEATH.

check.q: What does memento mori mean?
check.why: The reading says memento mori is Latin for remember that you will die.

check.q: What was the goal of a memento mori message?
choices: To scare children away from graves
To remind people to live well and use their time wisely
To hide the location of treasure
To give directions to the church
check.why: The reading says the idea was to live well, be kind and use time wisely.

lessons.title: Why Put Code on a Grave?
lessons.mainIdea: A cipher on a gravestone can be a message for friends who share a secret, not a treasure clue.
reading: A gravestone is public. Anyone can walk by and look. So why carve words that most people cannot read? We do not have a letter from Leeson or his friends that explains it. Historians can only look at the clues.

One clue is the square and compass. Masons in the 1700s knew the pigpen cipher well. A line in pigpen could be a quiet message to fellow Masons. It said, in effect, "This man was one of us." It was a way of belonging, like a team handshake.

Some people online claim the stone hides a treasure map. There is no evidence for that. The decoded words are a common saying about life and death. When a message is solved, it is wise to trust what the letters say. A good *historian* asks for evidence before believing an exciting story.

words.d: a person who studies the past using evidence
facts or objects that help show whether something is true

look.title: Two Visitors Talk
look.text: Visitor 1: "This code must hide the way to buried gold!" Visitor 2: "The code says REMEMBER DEATH. That was a common grave saying. The Masonic symbol suggests it was a message for other Masons."
look.prompt: Which visitor uses evidence? Point to one fact each visitor gives or leaves out.

check.q: Why might Masons have used pigpen on Leeson's stone?
choices: To hide the way to gold
To keep the church from reading it
As a quiet message to fellow Masons who knew the cipher
Because they could not spell in English
check.why: The reading says a pigpen line could be a quiet message to other Masons, a way of belonging.

check.q: Is there evidence that the Leeson stone hides a treasure map?
choices: No, the decoded words are a common saying
Yes, the church found the gold
Yes, Leeson wrote a letter about it
No, because the stone has no carvings
check.why: The reading says there is no evidence for a treasure map. The words are a common saying about life and death.

check.q: What does a good historian do before believing an exciting story?
choices: Tells it to as many people as possible
Waits for someone famous to agree
check.why: The reading says a good historian asks for evidence first.

lessons.title: Substitution Ciphers
lessons.mainIdea: In a substitution cipher, every letter is swapped for another letter or symbol by the same rule.
reading: To substitute means to put one thing in place of another. A *substitution cipher* puts a new letter or symbol in place of each letter. Pigpen is a substitution cipher. Each letter is always swapped for the same shape.

A very old example comes from ancient Rome. The Roman writer Suetonius wrote about the life of Julius Caesar. He said Caesar sent private letters in a cipher. Each letter was moved a few places down the alphabet. Today this is called a *shift cipher*, or the Caesar cipher.

Here is how a shift of three works. A becomes D. B becomes E. C becomes F. So the word CAT becomes FDW. To read it, you shift each letter back three places. The rule is simple, and it stays the same for the whole message.

words.d: a cipher that swaps each letter for another letter or symbol, always by the same rule
a cipher that moves each letter the same number of places along the alphabet

look.title: A Roman Writer on Caesar's Letters
look.text: When Caesar had something private to say, he wrote it in cipher. He changed the order of the letters so no word could be made out. To read it, you put D in place of A, and do the same with the other letters.
look.cite: Suetonius, The Life of Julius Caesar (in The Lives of the Caesars), c. 121 CE
look.prompt: How many places did Caesar shift each letter? Use the clue about A and D to explain.

check.q: In a shift cipher with a shift of three, what does A become?
check.why: With a shift of three, A moves three places to D.

check.q: Who wrote about Caesar using a cipher?
check.why: The reading says the Roman writer Suetonius described Caesar's letters in cipher.

check.q: Why is pigpen a substitution cipher?
choices: Because each letter is always swapped for the same shape
Because it shifts letters by three
Because it was used in Rome
check.why: A substitution cipher swaps each letter by the same rule, and pigpen gives each letter the same shape every time.

lessons.title: The Key Opens the Lock
lessons.mainIdea: A key is the rule or chart that locks a message and unlocks it again, so it must be kept safe.
reading: Think of a locked diary. The lock keeps the pages private. The key opens it. A cipher works the same way. The *key* is the rule or chart that hides the message and brings it back.

For a shift cipher, the key is a number, like three. For pigpen, the key is the drawing of the grids and X shapes. The person sending the message and the person getting it both need the same key. Anyone else should not have it.

Here is a problem. The pigpen key has been printed in many books. Today almost anyone can find it. So pigpen hides a message only from people who have not learned it. A cipher is only as strong as the secret of its key.

words.d: the rule, number or chart used to hide a message and to read it again
to hide a message by turning its letters into cipher letters or symbols

look.title: Two Friends and a Key
look.text: Jada and Luis make a secret shift cipher. They agree on the key "five" at recess. Later, Jada writes a note using a shift of five. A classmate finds the note. He does not know the key, so he tries a shift of one, then two, then three.
look.prompt: How many tries might the classmate need to find the key? What could Jada and Luis do to make their cipher harder to break?

check.q: What is the key in a cipher?
choices: The first word of the message
The paper the message is written on
The person who breaks the code
The rule or chart used to hide and read the message
check.why: The reading says the key is the rule or chart that hides the message and brings it back.

check.q: Why is pigpen not very safe today?
choices: Its key has been printed in many books
It only works in New York
It can only be carved in stone
check.why: The reading says the pigpen key is printed in many books, so almost anyone can find it.

check.q: What is the key for a shift cipher?
check.why: The reading says the key for a shift cipher is a number that tells how far to move each letter.

lessons.title: Counting Letters
lessons.mainIdea: Some letters appear much more often than others, and counting them helps codebreakers crack a cipher.
reading: About 1,100 years ago, a scholar named al-Kindi lived in Baghdad. He wrote the oldest known guide to breaking ciphers. His big idea was to count. In any long piece of writing, some letters show up much more than others.

In English, the most common letter is E. Codebreakers measure it at about 12.7 out of every 100 letters. Next come T, A and O. Letters like Q and Z are rare. Counting how often each letter appears is called *frequency analysis*. Frequency means how often something happens.

Here is how it helps. Say a secret message uses the shape of a triangle more than any other symbol. That triangle probably stands for E. The codebreaker writes E above each triangle. One guess at a time, the message starts to open.

words.d: breaking a cipher by counting how often each letter or symbol appears
how often something happens

look.title: The Most Common Letters in English
look.cite: Robert Lewand, Cryptological Mathematics (Mathematical Association of America, 2000), English letter frequency table
look.prompt: About how many times more common is E than Z? What would you guess first if a symbol appeared a lot in a secret message?

check.q: Which letter is the most common in English?
check.why: The reading says E is the most common letter in English, about 12.7 out of every 100 letters.

check.q: Who wrote the oldest known guide to breaking ciphers?
check.why: The reading says al-Kindi of Baghdad wrote the oldest known guide to breaking ciphers.

check.q: If one symbol appears most often in a long English message, what letter does it probably stand for?
check.why: Frequency analysis says the most common symbol probably stands for E, the most common English letter.

lessons.title: Clues From Short Words
lessons.mainIdea: Codebreakers mix letter counts with clues from short words and patterns to test their guesses.
reading: Counting letters is a great start, but it is not the whole job. Short messages can trick you. In REMEMBER DEATH, E is most common, which fits. But a short note about a zoo might have lots of Z and O. So codebreakers look for more clues.

Short words are strong clues. In English, a one-letter word is almost always A or I. A common three-letter word is THE. If a message has the same three symbols again and again, they may spell THE. Then you know T, H and E all at once.

Codebreakers also look for *patterns*. A double symbol, like in the middle of LOOK or BALL, is often O, E, L, S or T. Each guess is tested against the whole message. If a guess makes real words, keep it. If not, try again. Mistakes are part of the work.

words.d: something that repeats in a way you can notice and use
trying an answer, testing it, and changing it if it does not work

look.title: A Three-Symbol Clue
look.text: A secret message has the symbol group star, moon, box five times. Each time it stands alone as a three-letter word. The box is also the most common symbol in the whole message.
look.prompt: What word might star, moon, box spell? Which three letters would you now know? Explain your thinking.

check.q: In English, a one-letter word is almost always which letter?
check.why: The reading says a one-letter word in English is almost always A or I.

check.q: Why can counting letters trick you in a short message?
choices: Short messages may not follow the usual pattern
Short messages cannot be written in pigpen
Short messages always use a key
check.why: The reading gives the example of a short note about a zoo, which might have lots of Z and O.

check.q: What should a codebreaker do if a guess does not make real words?
check.why: The reading says to test each guess. If it does not make real words, try again.

lessons.title: Make and Break a Code Together
lessons.mainIdea: Codebreaking works best as teamwork, where each person spots different clues and checks the others' guesses.
reading: Now it is your turn. Your class can split into two teams. Team One makes a message. They choose a short sentence, maybe ten to fifteen words. They pick a cipher, such as a shift cipher or their own symbol alphabet. They keep the key hidden.

Team Two gets only the ciphertext. First, they count each symbol and make a tally chart. Next, they look for one-letter words and repeating groups. One person can track guesses on the board. Another can read the message aloud as it changes.

Real codebreakers work in teams too. One person may be good at counting. Another may notice patterns or know many words. When the message is solved, both teams can talk. What made it hard? What gave it away? *Teamwork* makes both sides stronger.

words.d: a chart that uses marks to count how many times something appears
people working together, each adding their own strengths

look.title: Plan Your Code Challenge
look.text: Team One writes the plaintext: I LIKE TO READ BOOKS AT THE LIBRARY. They choose a shift of four. Team Two will get only the ciphertext. They will have a tally chart, the board and a timer that is turned off, so no one feels rushed.
look.prompt: What clue do you think Team Two will spot first? Name one short word or pattern that could give the message away.

check.q: What does Team Two get at the start of the challenge?
check.why: The reading says Team Two gets only the ciphertext and must break it.

check.q: What is a tally chart used for in codebreaking?
choices: Counting how many times each symbol appears
check.why: A tally chart counts how often each symbol appears, which is the first step of frequency analysis.

check.q: Why do codebreakers often work in teams?
choices: Each person can spot different clues
One person is never allowed to read a cipher
Teams do not need to check guesses
check.why: The reading says one person may be good at counting and another at noticing patterns, so teamwork helps.

review.q: How do you write a letter in the pigpen cipher?
choices: Draw the shape of the letter's space on the grid or X
Write the next letter in the alphabet
Write a number for the letter
review.why: In pigpen, each letter is written as the shape of its pen, or space, on the key.

review.q: Which statement about the history of pigpen fits the evidence?
choices: Julius Caesar invented it in Rome
It was first carved on the Leeson stone
A grid for letters appears in the 1530s, and Masons later used it widely
review.why: Agrippa's book from the 1530s shows a letter grid. Masons took it up and spread it from the 1700s.

review.q: What does the pigpen line on James Leeson's stone say?
review.why: Decoded with the key, the line reads REMEMBER DEATH, a memento mori message.

review.q: What is the difference between plaintext and ciphertext?
choices: Plaintext is in pigpen and ciphertext is in English
Plaintext is the plain message and ciphertext is the hidden one
Plaintext is typed and ciphertext is handwritten
review.why: Plaintext is the message before it is hidden. Ciphertext is the message after it is hidden.

review.q: In a shift cipher with a shift of three, what does the word CAT become?
review.why: Each letter moves three places: C to F, A to D, T to W. So CAT becomes FDW.

review.q: What did al-Kindi teach codebreakers to do?
review.why: al-Kindi of Baghdad wrote about counting letters, which we now call frequency analysis.

review.q: A long English message in cipher uses one symbol far more than any other. What is the best first guess?
choices: It is a space and means nothing
review.why: E is the most common letter in English, so the most common symbol probably stands for E.

review.q: Why is it wise to ask for evidence before believing that a code hides treasure?
choices: Because exciting stories are not always true, and evidence shows what is
Because historians do not like stories
review.why: The Leeson stone lesson shows that the decoded words, not the exciting story, are the evidence.

chapters.title: The Copiale Cipher and the Art of Memory
chapters.bigQuestion: How do people and tools work together to unlock a secret, and how do people remember what they cannot write down?

story.title: A Book Nobody Could Read
story.kicker: Three researchers in two countries stare at a handwritten book that nobody had read for almost 300 years.
paragraphs: Picture a small book with a green and gold cover. Its pages are filled with neat handwriting. But the writing makes no sense. There are strange symbols mixed with ordinary letters. Some symbols look like arrows. Some look like tiny triangles or hooks. Page after page, the lines go on.

Someone wrote this book long ago, in the 1700s. Then, for almost 300 years, nobody could read it. People looked at it and wondered. Was it a secret diary? A book of magic? A list of hidden treasure? Nobody knew.

In 2011, three researchers decided to try. Kevin Knight worked at the University of Southern California, in the United States. Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer worked at Uppsala University, in Sweden. They were far apart, but they shared their work and their ideas.

Knight used computers to count and compare the symbols. Megyesi and Schaefer knew a lot about languages and old writing. Slowly, the pieces began to fit. The book was written in German. And it told the secrets of a society that cared a great deal about eyes.
In this chapter, you will follow how they cracked the Copiale Cipher. You will also meet stonemasons in Scotland. They were tested on something surprising: their memory.
story.think: The researchers lived in two different countries. How do you think that helped or made their work harder?

lessons.title: A Book Full of Symbols
lessons.mainIdea: The Copiale Cipher is a 105-page handwritten book from about 1730, written in a mix of symbols and letters.
reading: The *Copiale Cipher* is a real book. It has 105 handwritten pages. Its cover is made of green and gold patterned paper. Experts at Stockholm University say it was written around 1730. That makes it almost 300 years old.

The book holds about 75,000 written characters. A character is any single mark, like a letter or a symbol. The writer used about 90 different symbols. Some are ordinary letters from the Roman alphabet. Others are shapes nobody had seen in any book before.

Think about that number. English has only 26 letters. So why would a writer need about 90 symbols? That big number was one of the first clues. It told the researchers that this was not a simple swap of one letter for one symbol.

words.d: a secret handwritten book from about 1730, cracked in 2011
any single written mark, such as a letter, number or symbol

look.title: Counting the Copiale
look.cite: Stockholm University, "The Copiale Cipher" research project page (Decipherment of Historical Manuscripts)
look.prompt: How many more symbols did the Copiale use than the English alphabet has letters? What might the extra symbols be for?

check.q: About when was the Copiale Cipher written?
check.why: The reading says experts at Stockholm University date the book to around 1730.

check.q: How many pages does the Copiale Cipher have?
check.why: The reading says the book has 105 handwritten pages.

check.q: Why was the number of symbols, about 90, an important clue?
choices: It showed the book was written in English
It proved the book was a diary
It showed the book was very short
It showed the cipher was not a simple one-letter, one-symbol swap
check.why: English has only 26 letters, so about 90 symbols meant something more complex was going on.

lessons.title: Letters That Fooled Readers
lessons.mainIdea: In the Copiale, the plain letters were mostly a trick, and the real message hid in the symbols.
reading: When people first saw the Copiale, the Roman letters looked like the best place to start. They look like normal writing. But the researchers found they were mostly a trick. The team reported that the plain letters mostly served as spaces or *decoys*. A decoy is something meant to fool you.

The real message was hidden in the strange symbols and in letters with little marks above them. That is where the German words were. Readers who studied only the plain letters were looking in the wrong place.

The writer used one more trick. Common letters, like E, had several different symbols. This is called a *homophonic cipher*. It makes letter counting harder. If E is split among four symbols, no single symbol stands out as the most common one.

words.d: something meant to fool people and pull their attention away from the real thing
a cipher that gives common letters several different symbols, so counting is harder

look.title: Hide the E
look.text: Maria makes a cipher. She knows codebreakers look for the most common symbol to find E. So she gives E three symbols: a star, a moon and a heart. She switches between them as she writes. She also adds a few plain letters that mean nothing at all.
look.prompt: Which two Copiale tricks is Maria using? How would each trick slow down a codebreaker?

check.q: What was the main job of the plain Roman letters in the Copiale?
choices: They spelled out the whole message in English
They were mostly spaces or decoys
They gave the date of the book
check.why: The team reported that the plain letters were mostly spaces or decoys meant to fool readers.

check.q: Where was the real message hidden?
choices: Only in the plain Roman letters
In the strange symbols and marked letters
check.why: The reading says the German words were hidden in the symbols and in letters with small marks.

check.q: Why does a homophonic cipher make letter counting harder?
choices: It uses no vowels at all
Common letters are split among several symbols
check.why: When E has several symbols, no single symbol stands out as the most common.

lessons.title: Almost 300 Years Unread
lessons.mainIdea: The Copiale waited almost 300 years to be read, from about 1730 until it was cracked in 2011.
reading: Old books can sit on shelves for a very long time. The Copiale was written around 1730. It was cracked in 2011. That is a gap of almost 300 years. During that time, nobody we know of could read it.

A *timeline* helps you see a gap like that. Put the years in order on a line. Then you can compare them. For example, the Leeson stone in New York was carved after 1794. That is about 60 years after the Copiale was written.

Our timeline also shows an older event. In 1599, a Scottish official named William Schaw wrote rules for stonemasons. You will read about those rules later in this chapter. They asked masons to be tested on their *memory*.

words.d: a line that shows events in the order they happened
the power to keep and bring back things you have learned

look.title: Years on Our Timeline
look.cite: Second Schaw Statutes (1599); Stockholm University Copiale project page; Knight, Megyesi and Schaefer (2011); Leeson gravestone, Trinity Churchyard
look.prompt: About how many years passed between when the Copiale was written and when it was cracked? Show how you figured it out.

check.q: About how long did the Copiale go unread?
check.why: It was written around 1730 and cracked in 2011, a gap of almost 300 years.

check.q: Which event on the timeline came first?
check.why: The second Schaw Statutes are from 1599, the earliest year on the timeline.

check.q: What does a timeline help you do?
choices: See events in order and compare them
check.why: The reading says a timeline puts years in order so you can compare them.

lessons.title: What the Computer Did
lessons.mainIdea: Computers helped by counting symbols fast and comparing the patterns to real languages.
reading: Kevin Knight studies how computers work with human languages. For the Copiale, he first had the symbols typed into a computer. Each symbol got a name so the computer could track it. That took careful work by people.

Then the computer could do what it does best. It counted every symbol in seconds. It found which symbols came together often. It compared those patterns with patterns in many real languages. A person counting 75,000 characters by hand would need weeks.

The team's work pointed to German as the hidden language. But the computer did not understand German. It only matched patterns. People still had to test each guess and make sense of the words. A computer is a powerful *tool*, but it needs a thinking person to guide it.

words.d: something that helps a person do a job
facts and numbers collected so they can be studied

look.title: Fast Counter, Careful Thinker
look.text: Imagine this. A computer counts that one symbol appears thousands of times in the Copiale. It shows that this symbol often comes right before another one. It lists languages where two letters often come together like that. It cannot say what any word means.
look.prompt: What did the computer find? What must a person still do next? Name one job for each.

check.q: What was one thing the computer did well for the Copiale?
choices: Counted symbols quickly and compared patterns
Found the book in a library
check.why: The reading says the computer counted every symbol fast and compared patterns with real languages.

check.q: What language did the team's work point to?
check.why: The reading says the team's work pointed to German as the hidden language.

check.q: Why did the computer still need people?
choices: It was too slow at counting
It could not store the symbols
It only matched patterns and did not understand the words
check.why: The reading says the computer did not understand German. People had to test guesses and make sense of the words.

lessons.title: The Word for Eye
lessons.mainIdea: Beáta Megyesi noticed a symbol meaning "eye," and Christiane Schaefer linked it to a society called the Oculists.
reading: As German words began to appear, Beáta Megyesi noticed something. One symbol seemed to stand for a whole word: "eye." In German that word is Auge. The word eye seemed to come up again and again.

Why would a book care so much about eyes? Christiane Schaefer found the link. She connected the book to a secret society called the *Oculists*. The name comes from a Latin word for eye. It is also the root of the English word ocular, which means about the eyes.

That one small word opened the whole book. Once the team knew the subject, other words made sense. In 2011 they shared how they did it in a paper for other scientists. Many news reporters around the world told the story.

words.d: a secret society of the 1700s whose ceremonies were built around eyes and seeing
a connection between two things

look.title: The Team Reports Its Work
look.text: The researchers explain how they took apart a 105-page cipher book. They report that the hidden language was German. They say the book turned out to describe the ceremonies of a secret society in the 1700s.
look.cite: Kevin Knight, Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer, "The Copiale Cipher," Proceedings of the 4th Workshop on Building and Using Comparable Corpora, Association for Computational Linguistics, 2011
look.prompt: What two big facts did the team report? Why would other scientists want to read how they did it?

check.q: Which word did Beáta Megyesi notice?
check.why: The reading says Megyesi noticed a symbol that stood for the word eye, Auge in German.

check.q: Who linked the book to the Oculists?
check.why: The reading says Christiane Schaefer found the link to the society called the Oculists.

check.q: Where does the name Oculists come from?
check.why: The reading says the name comes from a Latin word for eye, like the English word ocular.

lessons.title: Why Teams Crack Codes
lessons.mainIdea: The Copiale was cracked because people with different strengths shared what they knew.
reading: Each person on the Copiale team brought something different. Knight knew how to make computers find patterns. Megyesi knew languages and how to study them with computers. Schaefer studies old languages and their history.

No one of them had every skill. Together, they did. This happens often in science and history. Big puzzles get solved when people share what they know. It is called *collaboration*, which means working together toward one goal.

Think about your own strengths. Maybe you notice tiny details. Maybe you remember words well. Maybe you stay calm when a puzzle is hard. Every one of those strengths helps a codebreaking team. Asking for help is also a skill.

words.d: working together with others toward one goal
something a person does well

look.title: Build a Dream Team
look.text: You need to crack a cipher written in Spanish. Ana speaks Spanish at home. Ben is great at counting and charts. Chen notices patterns that others miss. Dara reads old handwriting well.
look.prompt: What job would you give each person? Which Copiale researcher is each one most like?

check.q: What does collaboration mean?
check.why: The reading says collaboration means working together toward one goal.

check.q: Which skill did Christiane Schaefer bring to the team?
choices: Knowing about old languages and their history
check.why: The reading says Schaefer studies old languages and their history.

check.q: What is the main lesson of the Copiale team?
choices: Different strengths shared together can solve big puzzles
Computers work best with no people
check.why: The reading says no one had every skill, but together they did.

lessons.title: Who Were the Oculists?
lessons.mainIdea: The Oculists were a secret society in German-speaking lands whose ceremonies used the eye as a symbol for seeing truth.
reading: The decoded Copiale describes the *ceremonies* of the Oculists. A ceremony is a set of actions done in a special order for an important event. Many of these were for bringing in new members. The ceremonies were built around eyes and seeing.

Some summaries say the Oculists were a club of eye doctors. The researchers read it differently. They saw the eye as a symbol. To "see" meant to learn and understand the truth. People still talk this way. We say "I see" when we mean "I understand."

The Oculists seem to have been like the Freemasons in some ways. They met in secret, used symbols and had steps for joining. There were many clubs like this in Europe in the 1700s. The Copiale gives us a rare look inside one of them.

words.d: a set of actions done in a special order for an important event
the ceremony that brings a new member into a group

look.title: What Does It Mean to See?
look.text: Read these sentences. "I see what you mean." "She finally saw the answer." "Look at the problem with fresh eyes." None of them is about using your eyes to look at an object.
look.prompt: What does "see" mean in these sentences? How does this help explain why the Oculists used the eye as a symbol?

check.q: What do the decoded pages of the Copiale describe?
check.why: The reading says the decoded Copiale describes the ceremonies of the Oculists.

check.q: How did the researchers read the eye in the Oculists' ceremonies?
choices: As proof the members were all doctors
As a symbol for learning and seeing the truth
As a mistake in the cipher
check.why: The reading says the researchers saw the eye as a symbol for learning and understanding.

check.q: How were the Oculists like the Freemasons?
choices: They met in secret, used symbols and had steps for joining
check.why: The reading says the Oculists met in secret, used symbols and had steps for joining, like the Freemasons.

lessons.title: What the Secret Kept
lessons.mainIdea: The Copiale's secrets turned out to be ceremonies and lessons, not crimes or treasure.
reading: Before it was cracked, people could imagine anything about the Copiale. A hidden plot? A treasure? A dark crime? Secret books make people wonder. But when the words were read, they described ceremonies and lessons for members.

Members of groups like the Oculists had their own reasons for secrecy. The ceremonies felt special because they were private. New members did not know what was coming. That made the moment of joining feel important. Secrecy also helped members trust one another.

Outsiders often saw it another way. In the 1700s, some critics feared that secret clubs hid plots against rulers or churches. Those fears were real feelings. But in this case, the evidence shows the secret protected a ceremony. Historians let the evidence decide.

words.d: keeping something hidden from people outside a group
a person who points out problems or finds fault with something

look.title: Member and Critic
look.text: A member of a secret club says: "We keep our ceremony private so it feels special for each new friend." A critic says: "If a group hides its meetings, it might be planning something wrong."
look.prompt: What is each speaker worried about or proud of? For the Copiale, what does the evidence show?

check.q: What did the decoded Copiale turn out to contain?
check.why: The reading says the words described ceremonies and lessons for members.

check.q: Why did members of groups like the Oculists keep their ceremonies private?
choices: Because the ceremonies were against the law
Because private ceremonies felt special and built trust
Because the king told them to
check.why: The reading says privacy made joining feel special and helped members trust one another.

check.q: What did some critics in the 1700s fear about secret clubs?
choices: That they spent too much on candles
That they hid plots against rulers or churches
That they had too many members
check.why: The reading says some critics feared secret clubs hid plots against rulers or churches.

lessons.title: A Memory Test for Masons
lessons.mainIdea: In 1599, William Schaw's rules told Scottish masons to be tested on the art of memory.
reading: William Schaw was the Master of Works for King James VI of Scotland. That means he was in charge of the king's buildings. He also wrote rules for the lodges of stonemasons. These rules are called the *Schaw Statutes*. A statute is a written rule.

The first set came in December 1598. A second set followed in December 1599. One part spoke to the lodge at Kilwinning, a town in Scotland. It said the lodge leaders must test every skilled mason and every *apprentice* on "the art of memory." An apprentice is a person learning a trade.

The old Scots words say "airt of memorie." The rules even set a fine, a money penalty, for a mason who forgot. Why would builders be tested on memory? Masons had to keep a lot in their heads. They needed building skills. They also needed the rules and words of their lodge.

words.d: rules for Scottish stonemasons' lodges written by William Schaw in 1598 and 1599
a person who is learning a trade from a skilled worker
money a person must pay as a penalty for breaking a rule

look.title: The Kilwinning Rule
look.text: The leaders of the lodge at Kilwinning must test the art of memory, and the knowledge of it, of every skilled mason and every apprentice, each by their level. A mason who fails is to pay a fine.
look.cite: Second Schaw Statutes, signed by William Schaw, 28 December 1599 (modern English wording; see The Square magazine transcription, 2022)
look.prompt: Who had to be tested, and what happened to a mason who failed? Why might a lodge care so much about memory?

check.q: Who was William Schaw?
choices: The Master of Works for King James VI of Scotland
check.why: The reading says Schaw was Master of Works, in charge of the king's buildings.

check.q: What did the 1599 rules say the Kilwinning lodge must test?
choices: How well masons could read German
How many stones masons could lift
check.why: The reading says the rules told the lodge to test every mason and apprentice on the art of memory.

check.q: What happened to a mason who failed the memory test?
choices: He had to pay a fine
check.why: The reading says the rules set a fine, a money penalty, for a mason who forgot.

lessons.title: Memory Palaces
lessons.mainIdea: A memory palace is a way to remember things by placing them in a place you know well.
reading: An old story comes from ancient Greece. The Roman writer Cicero told it. A poet named Simonides was at a big dinner. He stepped outside, and the roof of the hall fell in. Simonides could name every guest by remembering where each one had sat. It is told as a legend, and it gave people an idea.

The idea is called a *memory palace*. You picture a place you know well, like your home. Then you "put" each thing you need to remember in a spot along the way. To remember, you take a walk in your mind. You find each thing where you left it.

What did Schaw mean by the art of memory? Historian David Stevenson thinks it may mean memory methods like this one. They were popular in Schaw's time. Other historians are not sure how far to take this idea. The rules do not explain the words, so the question stays open.

words.d: a way to remember things by picturing them in spots along a place you know well
an old story that is told as if it happened, but cannot be proved

look.title: A Walk Through Your Home
look.text: You need to remember three things: milk, a library book and a birthday card. Picture your front door with a giant carton of milk leaning on it. On the couch, a library book is reading itself. In the kitchen, a birthday card is singing.
look.prompt: Close your eyes and walk through the three spots. Can you name all three things? Which picture was easiest to remember, and why?

check.q: In the old story, how did Simonides name the guests?
choices: He remembered where each one had sat
He found their names on cards
check.why: The legend says Simonides named every guest by remembering where each one sat.

check.q: How does a memory palace work?
choices: You picture things in spots along a place you know well
You repeat one word many times
check.why: The reading says you picture each thing in a spot in a familiar place, then walk through it in your mind.

check.q: What do historians say about the meaning of "the art of memory" in Schaw's rules?
choices: Everyone agrees it meant spelling tests
It meant carving names on stones
David Stevenson thinks it may mean memory methods, but others are not sure
check.why: The reading says Stevenson links it to memory methods, others are not sure, and the question stays open.

lessons.title: Codes That Help You Remember
lessons.mainIdea: Masons later kept pocket-size books in cipher to help them remember their ceremonies, joining codes and memory.
reading: Codes and memory worked together for Masons. Masons were expected to learn their ceremonies by heart. That is a lot of words to remember. So some kept small books to help them study.

The Scottish Rite Masonic Museum and Library in Lexington, Massachusetts, keeps several of these books. One is a pocket-size notebook in *cipher*. Another is a whole ceremony book in cipher from about 1920. Masons saw them as private study helps. Critics saw them as proof of hidden secrets.

You can use both tools too. Try a memory palace for spelling words or science facts. Or make a small study card in your own cipher. Everyone learns in their own way. Pictures, places, codes and practice can all help your brain hold on to ideas.

words.d: a way of hiding a message by changing each letter into another letter or symbol
something that helps a person learn and remember

look.title: Build Your Classroom Palace
look.text: Pick five spots in your classroom in order: the door, the pencil sharpener, the window, the bookshelf and your desk. Now pick five facts from this unit. Place one fact at each spot as a funny picture. For example, a giant pigpen grid could hang on the door.
look.prompt: What five facts did you place, and where? Walk through your palace and say them aloud to a partner.

check.q: Why did some Masons keep small books in cipher?
choices: To help them study and remember their ceremonies
check.why: The reading says Masons had to learn ceremonies by heart and kept small books in cipher to help them study.

check.q: Where can you find a Masonic ceremony book in cipher from about 1920?
choices: The Scottish Rite Masonic Museum and Library in Lexington, Massachusetts
check.why: The reading says that museum and library in Lexington keeps these cipher books.

check.q: How did critics see the Masons' cipher books?
choices: As a new kind of art
check.why: The reading says Masons saw them as study helps, but critics saw them as proof of hidden secrets.

choices: A handwritten book from about 1730 in a mix of symbols and letters
A set of rules for Scottish masons
review.why: The Copiale is a 105-page handwritten book from about 1730, written in symbols and letters.

review.q: Who cracked the Copiale Cipher in 2011?
choices: Kevin Knight, Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer
William Schaw and King James VI
review.why: The chapter names Knight, from the United States, and Megyesi and Schaefer, from Sweden.

review.q: Which trick did the Copiale writer use to fool readers?
choices: Mixing in plain letters that were mostly decoys
review.why: The team reported that the plain Roman letters were mostly spaces or decoys.

review.q: How is the Copiale's homophonic cipher different from pigpen?
choices: Pigpen gives common letters many symbols
The Copiale gives common letters several symbols, but pigpen gives each letter one shape
They work exactly the same way
review.why: Pigpen gives each letter one shape. The Copiale split common letters among several symbols.

review.q: What small word helped open the whole Copiale book?
review.why: Megyesi noticed a symbol for eye, and Schaefer linked it to the Oculists.

review.q: What do the decoded pages of the Copiale show about the Oculists' secret?
choices: It hid a plan to rob a bank
It hid a list of eye doctors' patients
It protected ceremonies and lessons for members
review.why: When the book was read, it described ceremonies, not crimes or treasure.

review.q: What did the second Schaw Statutes of 1599 ask the Kilwinning lodge to do?
choices: Test masons and apprentices on the art of memory
Build a castle for the king
review.why: The 1599 rules told Kilwinning's leaders to test every mason and apprentice on the art of memory.

review.q: What is true about the link between Schaw's "art of memory" and memory palaces?
choices: Schaw wrote a book about memory palaces
Historian David Stevenson suggests a link, but historians are not all sure
The link is proved by the Copiale
review.why: Stevenson thinks the art of memory may mean methods like memory palaces, but the question stays open.
